candidates.title: Opinion: Congress should provide sustained funding for grade-crossing elimination
candidates.excerpt: Trains Turntable: Commentary from Association of American Railroads CEO Ian Jefferies For 10 years, See Tracks? Think Train Week has reminded Americans of a simple but essential fact: railroad tracks are not places to take chances with your safety. This annual campaign has helped raise awareness about the dangers for drivers and pedestrians around railroad tracks and crossings. But as we mark its 10th anniversary, we should also recognize that the most effective way to prevent collisions at highway-rail crossings is to eliminate the crossing altogether. That is why Congress should provide sustained, robust funding for the Railroad Crossing Elimination (RCE) Grant Program. Every one of the nation’s 200,000 grade crossings presents a potential point of conflict between trains, vehicles, and pedestrians. candidates.title: Another chance for Cotton Belt 4-8-4 No. 819
candidates.excerpt: PINE BLUFF, Ark. — Another pleasant surprise in the world of mainline steam for 2026: The Arkansas Railroad Museum and its parent organization, Cotton Belt Rail Historical Society, announced Sept. 24 that they have launched an evaluation to determine what would be required to return St. Louis Southwestern Railway (Cotton Belt) 4-8-4 No. 819 to service. The home-built 4-8-4 was pulled outside its birthplace, the museum’s former Cotton Belt shops, on Sept. 22 for a comprehensive inspection at the hands of Rail Dynamics Group (RDG). The assessment will establish the locomotive’s present condition, identify necessary work, estimate costs, and explore how the work itself could be accomplished. Rolled out in 1943 from the same facility it now calls home, No. 819 is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has been designated as Arkansas’ official state locomotive. candidates.title: CU Lines orders two 14,000 TEU container ships
candidates.excerpt: China United Lines (CU Lines) has placed an order for two 14,000 TEU container ships at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding. The newbuildings are scheduled for delivery during 2028 and 2029. The vessels will become the largest ships ever operated by CU Lines. The carrier’s biggest owned vessels currently have a capacity of 6,400 TEU. It also operates one chartered container ship of 10,100 TEU. The order therefore represents a major expansion in vessel size for the Chinese carrier.

candidates.title: Iran considers selling seized vessels to fund conflict compensation
candidates.excerpt: Iran has indicated that vessels seized over alleged links to the United States and Israel could be sold to compensate people affected by the recent conflict. Shipping reports have identified the container ships MSC Francesca and Epaminondas among the vessels potentially concerned. However, no final decision regarding their sale has been announced, as reported by DynaLiners. Separately, Iran’s judiciary said assets connected with MSC Aries could also be used to fund compensation once ongoing legal proceedings are completed. Iranian authorities seized MSC Aries in April 2024. The country links the vessel to Israeli shipowner Eyal Ofer and Zodiac Maritime. Any sale or transfer of assets would remain subject to the relevant court decisions in Iran.

candidates.title: Maersk confirms order for 26 18,600 TEU vessels
candidates.excerpt: Maersk has confirmed an order for 26 LNG-fuelled container ships, each with a capacity of 18,600 TEU. According to DynaLiners, the agreement follows earlier market speculation that the Danish carrier was considering up to 42 new vessels with capacities ranging from 18,000 to 24,000 TEU. The confirmed order will add approximately 484,000 TEU of capacity. It will also expand Maersk’s current orderbook by around 28%, bringing the total close to 2.2 million TEU. Details regarding the selected shipyards and the value of the contracts have not yet been disclosed. The vessels are expected to be delivered during 2029 and 2030.

candidates.title: Container ship fleet set to grow 9% in 2027 as supply pressure mounts
candidates.excerpt: The container shipping market could face increasing supply pressure in 2027 as fleet growth accelerates and new vessel deliveries continue to enter the market, according to BIMCO’s latest Container Shipping Market Overview & Outlook. BIMCO published its September 2026 outlook on 23 September under the headline “Supply pressure is mounting.” The organisation expects container fleet capacity to grow by 4.6% in 2026 before accelerating to 9% in 2027. The outlook comes as the global container fleet has already reached around 34 million TEUs. Meanwhile, the container ship orderbook now exceeds 14 million TEUs, equivalent to around 42% of the existing fleet. BIMCO expects recycling activity to remain low, which means new vessel deliveries will translate into faster overall fleet growth. Container volumes rise 5.1% Demand has remained relatively strong during 2026. According to BIMCO, global container volumes increased by 5.1% year-on-year during the first seven months of the year. candidates.excerpt: Germany’s Offen Group is looking to return to containership newbuildings after more than a decade away, with the Hamburg tonnage provider linked to up to four ships at China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International. Shipbroking and market sources have Offen in discussions with the CSSC-controlled yard for two firm plus two optional 7,000 teu vessels, with delivery slots pencilled in for 2030. The project remains under negotiation and no contract, pricing or propulsion details have yet been confirmed. A deal would mark Offen’s first containership newbuilding programme in more than 10 years and bring fresh tonnage into a fleet where much of its post-panamax exposure is now well into its second decade. The company’s own fleet pages describe Offen as Germany’s largest non-operating containership owner, managing more than 40 ships across panamax, post-panamax and super-post-panamax sizes. candidates.title: New container shipping route launched between E.China’s Jiangsu and Mexico
candidates.excerpt: New container shipping route launched between E.China’s Jiangsu and Mexico A cargo ship carrying 524 special containers departed from Jiangyin port in East China’s Jiangsu Province on Wednesday for Port of Manzanillo in Mexico, marking the official launch of a new direct container shipping route linking Jiangsu and Mexico. This new route operates as a direct service with a voyage time of approximately 22 days. Compared with the traditional shipping routes that require transshipment via Shanghai, Ningbo and other ports, the new route greatly cuts down cargo transit time and reduces logistics costs. The route provides a more efficient and convenient maritime passage for enterprises in the Yangtze River Delta seeking to expand in the North American market, a China News Service report said, citing Jia Yabo, deputy head of the local Maritime Safety Administration. candidates.title: Global disruption puts resilience of maritime trade in focus, says DP World
candidates.excerpt: Global disruption puts resilience of maritime trade in focus, says DP World More than 80% of world merchandise trade by volume is transported by sea. The networks carrying an estimated $14 trillion worth of containerised goods are being tested by geopolitical disruption, climate pressures and changing trade policies. A new whitepaper published by DP World’s Marine Services business to mark World Maritime Day 2026, examines how these forces are reshaping global cargo flows, and why more connected, adaptable trade corridors are becoming critical to keeping goods moving. As established shipping routes come under increasing pressure, businesses need greater choice in how cargo moves between markets. These shifts are creating a growing role for feeder, coastal and shortsea shipping solutions in connecting emerging production centres and regional ports to major international trade lanes. candidates.excerpt: Rail traffic on U.S. carriers came to 535,663 carloads and intermodal units, up 4.9% compared with the same week last year, according to Association of American Railroads data for the week ending Sept. 19. Total carloads reached 234,207 units, up 2.4%, while intermodal volume was 301,456 containers and trailers, better by 6.9% compared to 2025. Seven of the 10 carload commodity groups posted an increase compared with the same week in 2025. Metallic ores and metals surged 15.1%, followed by petroleum and petroleum products, 12.5%, and nonmetallic minerals such as sand and stone, 7%. Grain paused its long stretch of gains, down 7.7%, joined by losses in coal, 3.1%, and motor vehicles and parts, 0.8%. Through the first 37 weeks of the year, U.S. railroads reported cumulative volume of 8,444,095 carloads, up 2.7%, and 10,477,086 intermodal units, up 4.1%, y/y.
